questions.prompt: In the negative-feedback block diagram, the summing junction forms the error signal \(s_{err}\). Which expression gives it?
options: \(s_{err} = s_{in} - f\,s_{out}\)
\(s_{err} = s_{in} + f\,s_{out}\)
\(s_{err} = s_{in} - s_{out}/f\)
questions.explanation:
The feedback block \(f\) takes a fraction of the output, \(f\,s_{out}\), and the junction SUBTRACTS it from the input (that is what 'negative' feedback means): \(s_{err}=s_{in}-f\,s_{out}\).
• Adding \(f\,s_{out}\) would be positive feedback.
• \(G\) multiplies the error afterwards; it is not part of the subtraction.
• Dividing by \(f\) mixes up which direction the signal travels in the loop.

questions.prompt: In the standard negative-feedback diagram, which block does the error signal enter?
questions.explanation: The summing junction builds the error, and that error is the input of the forward block. The feedback block takes the output, not the error. Nothing in the diagram drives the reference arrow backwards.

questions.prompt: Order a trip around the negative-feedback diagram, starting at the summing junction.
questions.explanation: Negative feedback subtracts first, then drives the forward block, then samples the output, then returns that sample to the minus sign. Starting at the feedback block skips the error. Adding at the junction would be the other sign.

questions.prompt: The reference is \(r\) and the signal returned by the feedback block is \(b\). Write the error for negative feedback, using the names \(r\) and \(b\).
questions.explanation: Negative feedback subtracts the returned signal from the reference: \(r-b\). Adding them is positive feedback. Dividing \(r\) by \(b\) is not what the junction does.

questions.prompt: The reference is \(5\) and the feedback block returns \(2\) to a subtracting junction. What is the error?
questions.explanation: The junction subtracts: \(5-2=3\). Adding the two signals gives \(7\), which would be the positive-feedback error. The returned signal \(2\) is not the error.

questions.prompt: What does the minus sign on the feedback input of the summing junction mean?
questions.explanation: The minus sign is the subtraction that makes the feedback negative. It does not by itself invert the forward block, force the output below the reference, or set the feedback-block gain.

questions.prompt: A sketch of a negative-feedback diagram is described in four steps. Exactly one step is wrong.
questions.explanation: The first three steps are the negative-feedback diagram. The last step adds the return, which is the positive-feedback junction. The error of a subtracting junction is the reference minus the returned signal.

questions.prompt: The output is \(8\) and the feedback block has gain \(0.25\). What signal does that block return to the summing junction?
questions.explanation: The feedback block multiplies the output: \(0.25 \times 8 = 2\). The output \(8\) is not the returned signal, and \(8/0.25=32\) runs the block backwards.

questions.prompt: Which statements describe the negative-feedback diagram?
questions.explanation: The error drives the forward block, and the output drives the feedback block. Two plus signs would be positive feedback. The reference is an input of the junction, not an output of the forward block.

questions.prompt: Preview of loop gain. The forward block has gain \(4\) and the feedback block has gain \(0.5\). What is the product of those two gains?
questions.explanation: One trip around the loop multiplies the two blocks: \(4 \times 0.5 = 2\). A later skill names that product the loop gain. The sum \(4.5\) is not the trip, and \(4/0.5=8\) divides the blocks.

questions.prompt: Preview of open-loop and closed-loop behavior. A room heater is adjusted from a measured temperature. Which block is the thermometer?
questions.explanation: The thermometer samples the room, so it is the feedback block. The heater plus the room is the forward block. The junction compares the setpoint with the measurement. The setpoint itself is the reference, not a sensor.

questions.prompt: Preview of block-diagram algebra. Two forward blocks in series have gains \(3\) and \(4\). A later reduction replaces them by one block. What is that block's gain?
questions.explanation: Blocks in series multiply: \(3 \times 4 = 12\). A later skill uses that product when it collapses a diagram. Adding the gains is a parallel combination, and a ratio would be one block driven backwards.

retired_questions.prompt: A feedback system has forward gain \(G\) and feedback factor \(f\). When \(Gf \gg 1\), the closed-loop gain \(G/(1+Gf)\) approaches
options: \(G\), the forward gain
\(Gf\), the loop gain
\(1/f\), which does not depend on \(G\)
retired_questions.explanation:
If \(Gf\gg1\) then \(1+Gf\approx Gf\), so \(\dfrac{G}{1+Gf}\approx\dfrac{G}{Gf}=\dfrac1f\). The gain is set by the feedback network alone, so even a sloppy, drifting \(G\) gives a precise closed-loop gain.
• Closed-loop gain \(\approx G\) would only happen if \(Gf\ll1\) (almost no feedback).
• \(Gf\) is the gain around the loop, not the gain from input to output.

retired_questions.prompt: A feedback system has forward gain \(G=1000\) and feedback factor \(f=0.1\). What is the closed-loop gain \(s_{out}/s_{in}\)?
retired_questions.explanation:
\(G_{closed}=\dfrac{G}{1+Gf}=\dfrac{1000}{1+1000\cdot0.1}=\dfrac{1000}{101}=9.901\).
Compare with the shortcut \(1/f=10\): since \(Gf=100\gg1\), the shortcut is within 1%. Common mistake: forgetting the 1 in the denominator and answering \(G/(Gf)=10\) exactly.

retired_questions.prompt: A temperature control loop has forward gain \(G=40\) (°C per unit of command) and a sensor in the feedback path with \(f=0.5\) (units per °C). What is the closed-loop gain from setpoint command to temperature, in °C per unit?
retired_questions.explanation:
\(\dfrac{G}{1+Gf}=\dfrac{40}{1+20}=1.90\). The ideal value \(1/f=2\) is off by \(1/(1+Gf)=4.8\%\) because the loop gain of 20 is only moderate.
• 40 ignores the feedback.
• 2 is the infinite-loop-gain limit.
• \(40/(1+0.5)=26.7\) adds f instead of the loop gain \(Gf\).

retired_questions.prompt: A unity-feedback loop (\(f=1\)) has forward gain \(G=200\). The input is a constant 3. What is the size of the error signal \(e=x-fy\) at the summing junction after settling?
retired_questions.explanation:
\(e=\dfrac{x}{1+Gf}=\dfrac{3}{201}=0.0149\). The output is \(Ge=2.985\), almost equal to the input. A large loop gain drives the error close to zero, but never exactly to zero with finite G.
• 3 is the error with no feedback.
• \(3/200=0.015\) is close but uses G instead of \(1+Gf\).
• 0 would require infinite gain or an integrator.

retired_questions.prompt: In a feedback system with \(f=0.05\), the forward gain \(G\) drops by 10%, from 1000 to 900 (aging or temperature). About how much does the closed-loop gain change?
options: About 10%, the same as G
About 5%, half of G's change
About 0.2%, much less than 10%
About 2%
retired_questions.explanation:
Compute both: \(1000/(1+50)=19.61\) and \(900/(1+45)=19.57\). The change is \(0.22\%\).
In general \(\dfrac{dG_{cl}}{G_{cl}}=\dfrac{1}{1+Gf}\dfrac{dG}{G}\): feedback shrinks the sensitivity to \(G\) by the factor \(1+Gf\approx 50\), and \(10\%/50 = 0.2\%\). That is exactly why feedback is used for precision.
• 10% would be the no-feedback behavior.
• 5% and 2% don't match the factor \(1+Gf\approx50\).

retired_questions.prompt: As \(G\to\infty\), the error signal \(s_{err}=s_{in}/(1+Gf)\) of a negative-feedback loop goes to zero, yet the output \(s_{out}\) stays finite and equal to \(s_{in}/f\). How is that consistent?
options: The output must also go to zero, since \(s_{out}=G\,s_{err}\) and \(s_{err}\to0\)
\(s_{out}=G\,s_{err}\): a vanishing \(s_{err}\) times an enormous \(G\) leaves a finite product, \(s_{in}/f\)
The loop breaks, so the output is undefined for infinite \(G\)
\(s_{err}\) is exactly zero for any finite \(G\), so the output is exactly \(s_{in}/f\) even for small \(G\)
retired_questions.explanation:
\(s_{err}=s_{in}/(1+Gf)\) is never exactly zero for finite \(G\); it shrinks as \(1/G\). The output is \(G\cdot s_{err}=\dfrac{G}{1+Gf}s_{in}\to\dfrac{s_{in}}{f}\).
This is the origin of the 'golden rules' for op-amps: the input difference is ≈ 0 BECAUSE the gain is huge, while the output is whatever value makes the feedback signal \(f\,s_{out}\) equal \(s_{in}\). This is a '\(0\cdot\infty\)' limit.
• \(s_{out}\) cannot vanish: if it did, the feedback signal would be zero and the error would equal \(s_{in}\), contradicting \(s_{err}\to0\).
• The loop is perfectly well defined; the equation \(s_{out}=G(s_{in}-f s_{out})\) simply solves algebraically.

retired_questions.prompt: A designer accidentally makes the feedback POSITIVE: \(s_{err}=s_{in}+f\,s_{out}\). The loop gain is \(Gf=0.9\) with \(G=50\). What is the closed-loop gain \(G/(1-Gf)\)?
options: 500, ten times larger than \(G\), and very sensitive to small changes in \(Gf\)
26.3, the negative-feedback result
50, the same as \(G\)
Infinite, because positive feedback always blows up
retired_questions.explanation:
With positive feedback each trip around the loop adds a copy of the output: \(G_{closed}=G(1+T+T^2+\dots)=\dfrac{G}{1-T}\) for \(|T|<1\). Here \(T=0.9\), so \(G_{closed}=50/0.1=500\).
It is only infinite when \(T=1\) exactly, and it is hypersensitive near there: change \(T\) from 0.9 to 0.95 and the gain doubles to 1000. If \(T>1\) the output grows until something saturates ('railing out').
• \(50/(1+0.9)=26.3\) is the NEGATIVE-feedback answer.
• 'Always blows up' is false for \(T<1\).

retired_questions.prompt: A designer wants the closed-loop gain to be within 0.1% of the ideal value \(1/f\), i.e. \(G_{closed}\ge 0.999/f\). What is the minimum loop gain \(T=Gf\) needed?
retired_questions.explanation:
\(G_{closed}\cdot f=\dfrac{Gf}{1+Gf}=\dfrac{T}{1+T}\). Setting \(\dfrac{T}{1+T}=0.999\) gives \(T=\dfrac{0.999}{0.001}=999\).
So the loop gain must be about 1000 for 0.1% accuracy: the fractional error is \(\dfrac{1}{1+T}\). Common mistake: using \(T\ge0.999\).

retired_questions.prompt: Preview of control-system concepts. In a room thermostat, the forward block is 'heater plus room' and the feedback block is the thermometer. With a large loop gain, the room settles near setpoint\(/f\). If the thermometer reads 2% high (f is 2% too large), what happens?
options: Nothing: feedback cancels sensor errors as well
The room settles about 2% below the intended temperature, because the loop trusts the sensor
The room settles about 2% above the intended temperature
The loop becomes unstable
retired_questions.explanation:
With large loop gain the closed-loop gain is about \(1/f\), set by the feedback path. Feedback corrects errors inside the loop (plant drift, disturbances) but faithfully follows a biased measurement: a sensor reading 2% high makes the loop hold the true temperature about 2% low. This is why sensor accuracy matters more than actuator accuracy.
• Sensor errors sit in the feedback path, which is the one part feedback cannot correct.
• The direction is opposite: reading high means it stops heating too early.
• A 2% gain change does not affect stability here.

retired_questions.prompt: Preview of noise rejection. A disturbance of size 10 (for example a load change or a sensor offset) is injected at the forward block's OUTPUT, as in the figure, with \(s_{in}=0\). The loop has \(G=1000\) and \(f=0.05\). How large is the disturbance's contribution to \(s_{out}\)?
retired_questions.explanation:
With \(s_{in}=0\) and an additive disturbance, \(s_{out}=G(0-f\,s_{out})+s_{noise}\), so \(s_{out}=\dfrac{s_{noise}}{1+Gf}\).
Here \(Gf=50\), so \(s_{out}=\dfrac{10}{51}=0.196\). The loop 'sees' the disturbance as an error and fights it, rejecting it by the factor \(1+T\). Later skills (sensitivity and disturbance rejection) build on this.

retired_questions.prompt: Preview of bandwidth extension. The forward amplifier is \(G(s)=\dfrac{1000}{1+j\omega/\omega_p}\) with \(f_p=\omega_p/2\pi=1\ \mathrm{kHz}\), used inside a negative-feedback loop with \(f=0.1\). The closed-loop transfer function has the same one-pole form. Where is its pole, in kHz?
retired_questions.explanation:
\(G_{closed}=\dfrac{G}{1+Gf}=\dfrac{G_0/(1+j\omega/\omega_p)}{1+G_0f/(1+j\omega/\omega_p)}=\dfrac{G_0}{(1+j\omega/\omega_p)+G_0f}=\dfrac{G_0/(1+T_0)}{1+j\omega/[\omega_p(1+T_0)]}\) with \(T_0=G_0f=100\).
The pole moves up by the factor \(1+T_0=101\): \(f_{p,closed}=1\ \mathrm{kHz}\times101=101\ \mathrm{kHz}\). The DC gain dropped by the same factor (1000 → 9.9), so feedback trades gain for bandwidth, the idea behind the gain-bandwidth product.
